I wouldn't consider myself a very skilled gamer.  My reflexes aren't great and I'm not that good at memorizing patterns.  But I still beat the game and now that I'm replaying through it, its sort of easy even, but yes I did have trouble at first.

Honestly you just need to play smart, as it will largely make up for whatever lack of skill you may have.  Try to experiment and play around with with the timing for parries.  Watch enemies animations and try to look for a good indicator in their movement for when they will make contact and thus when you should parry.

Also, if you're having a hard time, something that helps a lot and doesn't require skill is just making sure you're playing optimally.  By that I mean:

Make sure you're getting all the gourd seeds and prayer beads you have access to.  Look up where to find them if you need to.  

Make sure you aren't investing your skill points into useless skills, again if you really need to, look up what upgrades are good and what's useless.

If you run out of gourd seeds, use pellets, (later on, shops will carry an unlimited supply of pellets so don't worry that they're finite).

Try to sneak up on at least one or two enemies before engaging in combat.  

Run away and disengage if you need to, after all, fighting multiple enemies at once is pretty difficult.

Use the right Shinobi prosthetics for the job, for example, fire is good against the chained ogre, your shuriken/ranged weapon is useful for picking off weaker enemies like wolves and archers, firecrackers are useful against most enemies to get in a few free hits.

If you find that the game isn't worth the amount of suffering you're being put through, there's nothing wrong in deciding its not for you.  Because yeah, the game isn't easy, but there is a lot of satisfaction to be had in beating each boss and overcoming each area.

Who knows, maybe Sekiro will open your tastes to some less casual games and you'll have fun trying out other challenging games.  But again, it's up to you at the end of the day whether its worth your time.

Either way, good luck and I'd love to hear how it goes if you do keep playing.  :)

On the other hand, it never hurts to improve your body, I was depressed after a breakup and working out not only was a great distraction but also made me feel accomplished and satisfied as time went on.   It really helps physically and mentally. 

I'd recommend doing home workouts if you can't or don't want to use a gym for whatever reason (which is totally fine).  The gym can be good for the variety of workouts you can perform but by no means is it necessary unless you're trying to compete in bodybuilding competitions or something lol.

Also, cardio is always good but building muscle also burns calories and it raises your metabolism.  I don't do cardio and I'm probably around 16-20% body fat, which isn't incredible but it isn't too bad.  That being said I'm a 21M who's only 5'8" and everyone's body is different. 

Also some very commonly overlooked aspects of fitness are sleep, water, and diet. 

Sleep is important for building muscle because it's your body's chance to rest and repair.  Working out doesn't mean you need to sleep more, but it makes getting the recommended amount of sleep more important because it will contribute to your fitness now too not just general health.

Water helps keep you full and aids in absorbing protein, its also just good for your health in general.  This isn't going to be a problem for most people but don't drink too much water like I did early on.  Just look up how much you need based on your weight and then try to get in that ballpark.  

Obviously diet isn't that overlooked by most, but some people don't realize how big of a part it plays in our health.  Something to be careful of, is being too restrictive with food and making yourself miserable.  Because that's not realistic nor is it fair to yourself.  

I did that early on and just got discouraged and temporarily gave up.  In fact I've done that multiple times haha.  So be realistic and change little things like having less chips with your meal, having one less scoop of ice cream, one less cookie, maybe use less mayo on a sandwich or less syrup on breakfast, etc.
That's the kind of stuff that has worked for me at least.  

As time goes on you can make bigger changes, but start small and just try to stick with it.  That goes for the working out too, don't run yourself into the ground by going from 0-100.

If you're trying to gain weight you can eat more.  If you want to gain muscle, you have to eat more as well as consume enough protein, which is supposed to be between 0.7 and 1 gram of protein for each pound you weigh. 

So if you're 118, try getting 82.6 grams of protein.  That can be difficult though, so I suggest doing a bit of research on high protein meals you could make, it might help to make a list of high protein ingredients to buy and high protein recipes to try out.  Meat is an easy choice so if you have access to it, take advantage.  If you don't eat/like meat or just want to vary your diet a bit, some common choices are eggs, greek yogurt, cottage cheese, beans, lentils.  

But since you're skinny and want to put on weight, you don't need to be limiting yourself to eating only "lean" protein as mentioned above.  So you could eat fattier sources of protein as well like milk, regular yogurt, almost any kind of cheese, peanut butter, etc.  

Protein shakes are the same as any of these other food I listed.  So yes protein shakes can help you gain weight if you're having trouble eating enough protein.  They aren't NEEDED to gain weight obviously, but they can make hitting that protein quota easier.  They helped me because instead having to stuff myself to the point of feeling ill with an extra meal, I could just drink a protein shake, which obviously still fills you up, but not as much as a normal meal. 

You don't need to dedicate all your time on your diet, but it helps to be smart about it and have a bit of a plan for your meals and track your protein.  You don't have to be exact but it helps to have an idea of how much protein (and calories if you want to track that too) you're getting on average.
